title: Dear Ijeawele, or A Feminist Manifesto in Fifteen Suggestions
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
target_audience: Parents and caregivers seeking to raise children with feminist values
Readers interested in gender equality and modern feminism
Educators and activists looking for accessible feminist resources
Fans of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s work
Individuals interested in intersectionality and contemporary African perspectives
primary_purpose: To offer practical, thoughtful, and accessible guidance on raising a child to value and embody feminist principles, in the form of fifteen actionable suggestions drawn from personal experience, culture, and contemporary feminist thought.

structure_format.organization: Begins as a personal letter to a friend (Ijeawele) responding to her request for tips on raising a feminist daughter, structured around fifteen clearly numbered suggestions, with supporting reflection and examples
features: Blend of theory and practical examples

key_concepts_lessons: Feminism is about equality, choice, and dignity for all genders.
Reject gender-based roles and expectations, both subtle and explicit.
Encourage a questioning attitude toward tradition and authority.
Language matters; avoid reinforcing gender stereotypes verbally or through books, toys, and media.
Teach children about consent, bodily autonomy, and respect.
Model feminist partnership and shared responsibility at home.
Value identity and self-worth beyond marital or relationship status.
Emphasize female ambition, self-reliance, and the right to anger or resistance.
Understand and resist social pressures to conform, especially as a woman.
Be conscious of intersectionality: recognize how culture, race, and class intersect with gender.
notable_features: Written in direct response to a personal, real-life query
Rooted in Nigerian and global feminist experience
Blends individual narrative and universal advice
Widely quoted in feminist and parenting circles
cultural_historical_context: Published in the wake of Adichie’s influential TEDx talk and essay 'We Should All Be Feminists,' the book responds to growing global conversations about gender equality, particularly around the #MeToo movement and increased attention to feminism in Africa and worldwide. It also addresses the realities of raising children in patriarchal societies.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for its clarity and conciseness
Frequently cited as a primer on modern, accessible feminism
Praised by parents and educators for practical wisdom
Used in schools, book clubs, and feminist groups as a guide
Some readers found it limited by its brief length and desired more depth
comparable_titles: We Should All Be Feminists by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
Feminist Fight Club by Jessica Bennett
The Mother of All Questions by Rebecca Solnit
